clue.text: All but spot on tar sand is processed with same aim

indicators.note: processing reworks raw material, so these letters are worked into a new order

explanation.surface: An oil company refining tar sands keeps the same goal, getting almost everything right.
explanation.walkthrough: 'is processed' rearranges the fourteen letters of TAR SAND and SAME AIM together; 'with' only joins the two fodder phrases. Tar sand is bitumen-soaked sand mined for oil.
explanation.definitionFit: Something all but spot on is very nearly exact, and the colloquial phrase means close enough to make no difference.

clue.text: Get to live around phosphorus plant

indicators.note: around puts one piece outside another

parts.note: to get something is to understand or see it
P is the chemical symbol for phosphorus
to dwell is to live somewhere

explanation.surface: Instructions to come and settle near a fertiliser rich in phosphorus.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Get' reads as a command, but it means grasp, as in 'I get it'; 'around' wraps that word round the chemical symbol.
explanation.definitionFit: A low-growing wild flower with small blue blooms, a common garden and hedgerow herb.

clue.text: Ancient people's commonest value getting overturned

indicators.note: in a down clue, overturned means turned upside down, so the word reads from bottom to top

parts.note: the mode is the most frequent value in a set of data

explanation.surface: An ancient people's most common value is turned on its head.
explanation.walkthrough: 's stands for 'is'. In statistics the mode is the value that occurs most often.
explanation.definitionFit: The biblical kingdom south of the Dead Sea gives its name to its people, the descendants of Esau.

clue.text: God with last letter published about Catholic form of coiffure

parts.note: Ra is the Egyptian sun god
Z is the last letter of the alphabet

indicators.note: about puts one piece around another

parts.note: out means published, as a book that is out
RC is the abbreviation for Roman Catholic

explanation.surface: A deity with an alphabet's final letter publishes something on a Catholic hairstyle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' wraps the publishing word round the church abbreviation. 'with last letter' sounds like a description of the god, but it supplies the final letter of the alphabet.
explanation.definitionFit: A hairstyle shaped with a razor rather than scissors, giving a tapered look.

clue.text: Try rattling opposing players and still end game completely gutted

indicators.note: gutting removes the insides, so each of the three words keeps only its first and last letters

explanation.surface: A team taunts its rivals and still ends up losing the match heavily.
explanation.walkthrough: S(til)L, E(n)D, G(am)E. In cricket, sledging means taunting batsmen to break their concentration.
explanation.definitionFit: A cricket verb for verbally needling the batting side to unsettle them.

clue.text: Desperately trawled for post-mortem location

indicators.note: something done desperately is wild and frantic, so the letters are thrown into a new order

explanation.surface: A fisherman trawled frantically, hunting for evidence after an autopsy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'post-mortem' looks medical, but here it means after death literally.
explanation.definitionFit: The realm the dead are believed to go to, the place you reach after dying.

clue.text: Who's uplifted Sound of Music with Mother Superior?

definitions.text: Who's uplifted Sound of Music with Mother Superior?

indicators.note: superior means placed above, so in this down entry the mother piece sits on top

parts.note: ma is a familiar word for mother

indicators.note: uplifted in a down entry means the word is read from bottom to top

parts.note: an air is a tune, the sound of music

explanation.surface: Who brightened The Sound of Music alongside the Mother Superior?
explanation.walkthrough: In the musical, the nuns ask how to solve a problem like her. AIR reversed is RIA, placed under MA.
explanation.definitionFit: The heroine of the musical, the novice nun whose spirits lift the film, works alongside the abbess.

clue.text: Hit out with dirt, end of the line in sordid hope for double loser?

indicators.note: out means knocked out of shape, so the letters are rearranged
in places the short pieces inside the word for sordid

parts.note: mucky means dirty or sordid

indicators.note: the end of the word means its final letter

explanation.surface: A slinger of dirt hopes the sordid tactic finally works after two defeats.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out' rearranges the first two words; 'in' places the final letter of 'the' and the line abbreviation inside the dirty word. A double loser has failed twice, so a third try is due to succeed.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who has failed twice consoles themselves with the saying that the next attempt will succeed.

clue.text: £25 to cover raised fees, left with plain brown wrapping under a false name

indicators.note: to cover means to go around the other piece

parts.note: a pony is British slang for twenty-five pounds

indicators.note: raised in a down entry means read from bottom to top

parts.note: dues are fees, such as membership dues

indicators.note: wrapping means one piece goes around the other

parts.note: mousy describes plain light brown hair

explanation.surface: Twenty-five pounds covers higher fees, delivered in plain brown paper under an assumed name.
explanation.walkthrough: 'raised' turns the fees word upside down in this down entry; 'to cover' and 'wrapping' each put one piece round another. 'Plain brown wrapping' suggests discreet mail-order packaging.
explanation.definitionFit: A writer using a pen name publishes without their real identity attached.

clue.text: Not quite drunk, crossing border in confusion

indicators.note: the shortened word lies across the other piece, holding it inside
not quite the whole word, so the final letter of the slang word for drunk is cut off

parts.note: sozzled is British slang for drunk
a hem is the folded border of a piece of cloth

explanation.surface: Someone tipsy but not fully drunk staggers over a frontier in a muddle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not quite' drops the final letter of the slang word for drunk, and 'crossing' sets the border inside what is left, just after its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A colloquial word for a muddled state of affairs or a noisy commotion, borrowed from Yiddish.

clue.text: Rare parts of statues found among collector's items

indicators.note: the letters sit among the words that follow, running across the break between them

explanation.surface: Unusual pieces of sculpture turn up in a collector's holdings.
explanation.walkthrough: The run straddles collecTOR'S Items. 'Rare' fits because the usual plural is torsos; the Italian-style plural is uncommon.
explanation.definitionFit: Statues often survive as trunks without head or limbs, and these trunks are named with an unusual plural form.

clue.text: Odd scraps of undercut, back and tongue

indicators.note: back tells us to read the picked letters in the other direction
the odd-numbered letters of the following word are the scraps kept

explanation.surface: A butcher offers oddments of undercut, back cuts and tongue.
explanation.walkthrough: The odd letters of UNDERCUT are U, D, R, U; 'back' turns them round. Undercut, back and tongue all sound like cuts of meat, but tongue is the definition: a language.
explanation.definitionFit: Tongue here means a language, and this one is spoken chiefly in Pakistan and India.

clue.text: Mission to fetch champagne? You'll want gold coin

parts.note: Krug is a famous champagne house
an errand is a short mission or task you are sent on

explanation.surface: Sent off to buy champagne, you'll need a pricey coin to pay for it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to fetch' and 'You'll want' are link words; the charade puts the champagne before the mission.
explanation.definitionFit: A South African bullion piece minted in gold and named after Paul Kruger and the rand currency.

clue.text: All but first pair of ducts around Embankment, erected without protecting Tube?

indicators.note: erected in a down entry means set upright, so the whole string reads from bottom to top
around means the shortened word surrounds the other piece
all of the word except its opening two letters is kept

parts.note: vessels are ducts that carry fluid in the body
a levee is a raised bank against river flooding

explanation.surface: Work on ducts round London's Embankment leaves an Underground line exposed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'All but first pair of' trims the ducts word, 'around' wraps it round the embankment, and 'erected' reads the lot upwards. The Embankment and Tube suggest London, but the tube is an arm's casing.
explanation.definitionFit: A garment with no arm coverings lacks the fabric tubes that would protect each arm.

clue.text: Deafening twosome see about gun's recoiling

indicators.note: recoiling, springing back like a gun, means the whole assembled string is read backwards

parts.note: a duo is a twosome

indicators.note: about places one piece around another

parts.note: lo is an old word meaning look or see
to gun an engine is to rev it

explanation.surface: A pair watch as a firearm kicks back with a deafening noise.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' puts the gun word inside the see word, and 'recoiling' turns the whole string backwards. 'gun' is a verb here, as in gunning an engine.
explanation.definitionFit: Deafening describes sound that is far too loud, which is just what the compound word means.

clue.text: One an elitist rebuffed, a specimen with restricted roots?

indicators.note: rebuffed suggests being pushed back, so the word for elitist is read backwards

parts.note: a snob is an elitist who looks down on others
an gives the indefinite article A
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: Someone is snubbed by a snob, much as a stunted plant is held back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rebuffed' turns the elitist word round. The question mark flags a definition by description: the miniature tree is kept small by pruning its roots in a shallow pot.
explanation.definitionFit: Japanese miniature trees are kept tiny by confining and pruning their root systems in small containers.

clue.text: Recreate conditions of surrounding temperature in fire

indicators.note: surrounding means the long word goes around the short piece

parts.note: to simulate is to recreate the conditions of something, as in a test

explanation.surface: Engineers recreate the heat of a blaze in a test chamber.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fire' looks like a noun but is a verb here: to fire up or rouse.
explanation.definitionFit: To fire someone's imagination is to rouse or excite it.

clue.text: Conform to standard expectations, declining a drink?

indicators.note: declining means turning down, so this letter is refused and dropped

parts.note: to be average is to conform to the norm

explanation.surface: Someone happy to be ordinary turns down a drink.
explanation.walkthrough: BE AVERAGE loses an A. The question mark marks a definition by example: a drink is one kind of the broader word.
explanation.definitionFit: Any liquid for drinking, such as tea, coffee or juice, falls under this general term.

clue.text: Deeply distressed, suddenly cried

indicators.note: distressed means damaged or roughed up, so the letters of the first word are knocked into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone in deep anguish let out a sudden cry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Deeply distressed' reads as one phrase describing a mood, but 'Deeply' is the fodder and 'distressed' rearranges it.
explanation.definitionFit: A dog that gives a sharp sudden squeal of pain has made exactly this kind of short high cry.

clue.text: Strike succeeded in bombardment for endless torment

indicators.note: to strike something out is to delete it, so a letter is crossed off

parts.note: shellfire is bombardment by artillery shells
S is the abbreviation for succeeded, used in genealogies

explanation.surface: A strike happens during a heavy artillery barrage that seems to go on forever.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Strike' looks like a noun for an attack, but it is an instruction to strike out the S from SHELLFIRE; 'in' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: The flames of hell are the traditional picture of eternal punishment for the damned.

clue.text: Possibly horse runners with heart sinking before one uncooked breakfast

indicators.note: before means the first piece comes ahead of the next
in a down entry, sinking means the central letter drops to the bottom of the word

parts.note: mules are hybrids bred from a horse, and they are used as pack runners, so possibly signals a loose example
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: Pack animals sink down before an uncooked breakfast.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with heart sinking' moves the middle L of MULES down to the end, giving MUESL.
explanation.definitionFit: A Swiss breakfast cereal of raw oats, nuts and dried fruit, eaten without cooking.

clue.text: Old Norse race eating hearts of horses after expelling knight unobtrusively

indicators.note: eating means one piece swallows the others inside it

parts.note: the TT is the Tourist Trophy motorcycle race on the Isle of Man
H is the abbreviation for hearts in card games

indicators.note: expelling throws a letter out of the word that follows

parts.note: equine means relating to horses
N is the chess notation for a knight

explanation.surface: Ancient Scandinavians at a race devour the hearts of horses once a knight is thrown out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hearts of horses' tempts you to take middle letters, but 'hearts' is the card abbreviation. 'after expelling' drops the knight from the horse word, and 'eating' puts both inside the Isle of Man race.
explanation.definitionFit: To do something unobtrusively is to do it secretly or discreetly, without drawing attention.

clue.text: River level going over top of banks

indicators.note: going over means wrapping across, so the level goes around the letter

parts.note: a tier is one level of a stack

indicators.note: the top of a word in a down entry is its first letter

explanation.surface: A river's level rises over the top of its banks.
explanation.walkthrough: B (top of 'banks') goes inside TIER. The river flows through Rome.
explanation.definitionFit: The great river of Italy that flows through Rome to the sea.

clue.text: Charm of couples at start of consecutive months

indicators.note: only a couple of letters at the start of each month are kept, the rest dropped

parts.note: June and July are months that follow one another

explanation.surface: A lucky charm consists of pairs of letters taken from back-to-back months.
explanation.walkthrough: The first two letters of JUNE and of JULY give the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A West African word for a magic charm or fetish, and by extension supernatural power or luck.

clue.text: Businesslike message from the writer on tick

indicators.note: on means placed above, in a down entry the first piece sits over the second

parts.note: the writer refers to the setter, giving ME
a tick is a moment, informally a mo

explanation.surface: A brief office note from me, written in an instant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tick' and 'mo' are both British slang for a moment.
explanation.definitionFit: A short written note circulated within an office or business.

clue.text: Slasher finishing neither cast down nor brought up

indicators.note: finishing means finishing off, taking away the final letter of each word

parts.note: cast down means downcast or sad
brought up means raised or bred

explanation.surface: A horror-film killer meets an end that is neither gloomy nor well raised.
explanation.walkthrough: 'neither ... nor' means both words lose their ends: SAD becomes SA and BRED becomes BRE.
explanation.definitionFit: A curved cavalry sword designed for cutting strokes, so a weapon that slashes.

clue.text: Soppy note on envelope involving step or steps away from gravity?

indicators.note: involving means taking the other piece inside it

parts.note: SWALK, sealed with a loving kiss, is a sentimental message written on the back of a love letter
a pace is a step

explanation.surface: A sentimental message on a love letter's envelope proposes a step away from serious matters.
explanation.walkthrough: SWALK, a British schoolchild's acronym for 'sealed with a loving kiss', is written on envelopes. 'gravity' suggests seriousness, but it is the physical force: astronauts step out beyond it.
explanation.definitionFit: An astronaut's excursion outside the spacecraft is a walk where gravity's usual pull is absent.

clue.text: Ladies up north sign on in other words and shirk working in wood

indicators.note: on means placed after, as the sign comes after the rest in an across entry
in places the combined pieces inside the tree name

parts.note: yew is a wood, from the evergreen tree
or is used to introduce a rephrasing, as in other words

indicators.note: working means the letters are worked into a new order

parts.note: an omen is a sign of what is to come

explanation.surface: Women from the north sign up, in other words, and dodge their jobs out in the woods.
explanation.walkthrough: 'working' rearranges shirk, 'in' puts it with the rephrasing word inside the tree, and 'on' adds the sign after. 'up north' is part of the definition, not a reversal signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Females from the largest county in northern England, the region the clue's phrase points to.
